Name: The Threat of Crucifixion for Defeated Commanders and the Alienation of Overseas Generals
RagShortTexts: Under Carthage's cruel military law, any defeated or derelict commander could be crucified by order of the Senate
Fearing the Senate's punishment, generals on the overseas fronts grew timid in battle or harbored divided loyalties
This extreme system of punishment left generals unwilling to take risks and deepened the mistrust between the front and the Council of One Hundred
BaseText: Carthage's constitution and military law kept a cruel Eastern survival: any general who suffered a major defeat abroad, lost a fleet or was judged to have fought poorly could be put to death on a cross by direct order of the Council of One Hundred. This bloody law was meant to stamp out cowardice and desertion in the face of the enemy, but in the Second Punic War it backfired disastrously. Overseas generals such as Bomilcar and Himilco knew that if they came home defeated they would surely face a cruel execution, so when the fighting was deadlocked they became extremely cautious and withdrew, preferring to watch allied armies be destroyed rather than risk a decisive battle; in moments of crisis some even secretly offered their loyalty to the enemy or abandoned their armies to save themselves. This noose hanging over the generals' heads gravely weakened the initiative of the Carthaginian army and the strategic coordination among its forces.

Variants.Content: In Rome, a defeated consul who returns to the city is still thanked by the Senate; in Carthage, the shadow of the cross hangs over our heads forever! How can anyone dare to risk everything?

Those given command squander the city's flesh and blood and vast wealth. If defeated generals are indulged, how can we console the brave men who died and the citizens who were ruined? The cross is the guarantee of order!

Rome treated the consul Varro leniently, because though defeated he did not despair; Carthage nails its generals to wooden stakes. The gap between barbarism and civilization is plain to see in their laws.
